title: Stack Frames, Calls and ABIs
subtitle: The universal shape that every language lowers to.
summary: Draw the x64 stack frame, learn SysV vs Win64 calling, and read objdump like prose.
learning_objectives: Draw a stack frame (high→low, return address, saved rbp, locals, 16-byte align).
Map a C function call to push/call/mov/sub/ret and explain callee vs caller saved registers.
Distinguish SysV AMD64, Win64, AAPCS64 and RISC-V calling conventions and their pitfalls.
prerequisites: Ability to run gcc -S and objdump

blocks.title: One picture to memorize
blocks.markdown: Every compiled language lowers calls to the same shape: caller pushes a return address, callee sets up a frame (`push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; sub rsp,N`), uses locals, tears down, and `ret` pops the address back. Get this picture and GDB backtraces stop being mysterious.

`call foo` pushes `RIP` (8 bytes) so the CPU knows where to return, then jumps. Inside `foo`, `push rbp` saves the caller's frame pointer, `mov rbp,rsp` makes the new base, `sub rsp,16` reserves locals while keeping 16-byte alignment for the next `call`. The debugger walks `saved rbp` links to show a backtrace. Forgetting the 16-byte rule makes `movaps` in the callee fault with #GP — a classic hand-written-assembly bug.

SysV leaf functions may use 128 bytes *below* `RSP` without adjusting `RSP` (red zone). Win64 requires 32 bytes of *shadow space* above the return address for the callee to spill registers — reserve it even if you don't use it.

blocks.alt: Interactive stack frame diagram showing high to low memory: arguments, return address, saved rbp, locals, alignment.
blocks.caption: Interactive — hover each box for what call/push/sub does. Click for ABI detail. Ctrl+wheel to zoom.

blocks.source:
; caller
call foo        ; push RIP (rsp-=8, [rsp]=ret), jmp foo
; foo prologue
push rbp
mov  rbp, rsp
sub  rsp, 16      ; locals, keep 16B align
mov  [rbp-8], rdi ; spill arg
; ... body ...
add  rsp, 16
pop  rbp
ret              ; pop RIP -> jmp back
blocks.explanation: Annotated x64 prologue/epilogue. High address at top, RSP grows down. RBP is the debugger's bookmark.

blocks.markdown: Calling conventions decide register ownership. SysV AMD64 callee must preserve `rbx, rbp, r12-r15`; Win64 preserves `rbx, rbp, rsi, rdi, r12-r15`; AAPCS64 preserves `x19-x28, SP`. Everything else is caller-clobbered. Clobbering a callee-saved register without restoring it corrupts the caller's data *after* the call returns — the bug appears one frame up, not inside the function you wrote.

blocks.alt: Table comparing SysV AMD64, Win64, AAPCS64 and RISC-V register arguments and preserved registers.
blocks.caption: System V vs Win64 vs AAPCS64 vs RISC-V. rdi/rsi/rdx etc. map to x0-x7 / a0-a7.

blocks.source:
cc -O0 -g add.c -c -o add.o
objdump -d add.o | less
cc -O2 add.c -S -o add.s && cat add.s
# try godbolt.org for ARM/RISC-V cross views
blocks.explanation: Build with and without optimisation; compare how -O2 removes the frame or inlines. Use Compiler Explorer for A64 (aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc) and RV64.

blocks.question: A leaf function under SysV uses [rsp-8] without sub rsp,8 and never calls another function. What allows this?
options: The compiler always pads stacks by 8.
The 128-byte red zone below RSP that leaf functions may use without adjusting RSP.
blocks.explanation: SysV defines a 128-byte red zone below RSP for leaf functions. Win64 has a different concept: 32-byte shadow space above the return address for spilling.

blocks.title: Read your own frame
blocks.objective: Write a C function, compile to assembly and map every instruction to the frame picture.
instructions: Write int add(int a,int b){ return a+b; } and int main that calls it.
Compile with -O0 -g and -O2 separately, dump with gcc -S and objdump -d.
Annotate where arguments arrive (rdi/rsi on SysV) and where the return leaves (rax).
Introduce a local array char buf[16]; observe sub rsp alignment.
Break with gdb, run bt and info reg rbp/rsp.
completion_criteria: You can draw your add's frame with addresses and register values
You state which registers are caller vs callee saved for your toolchain
